text:
Alex K.: Quick follow-up from the CP separation spike — proposing we split the connector into two logical roles: `edge-proxy` and `control-agent`.

Alex K.: Motivation: keep the control-plane surface minimal inside customer VPCs. `edge-proxy` handles north-south dataplane egress (TLS termination, connection pooling), `control-agent` handles handshake/authn and health checks.

Maria N.: +1 on principle. A couple questions: who owns retries/backoff logic? edge-proxy or control-agent? Also need clarity on cert refresh flow. :thinking_face:

Sam T.: My take: edge-proxy should be dumb for auth (bearer introspection only) and focused on performance + connection reuse. control-agent manages certs, rotation, and token refresh. That keeps hot path fast.

Rachel B.: Ops note: if control-agent does rotation you need a safe path for rolling certs without dropping established kv-cache streams. We had issues with abrupt mTLS restarts in staging.

Alex K.: Good call. Suggestion: control-agent exposes an in-process cache refresh endpoint that edge-proxy calls with zero-downtime semantics. Eg: edge-proxy keeps TCP connections open and switches TLS contexts on new connections only.

Maria N.: Can we show a small config sketch? makes it easier to reason about interfaces.

Alex K.: Sure — rough example: 

```yaml
connector: 
  role: edge-proxy
  listen: 0.0.0.0:443
  upstream: unix:/var/run/control-agent.sock
  auth: introspect-bearer
  conn_pool: 
    max: 500
    idle_timeout_s: 30
---
control-agent: 
  role: control-agent
  socket: /var/run/control-agent.sock
  cert_source: kms://redwood/certs/client
  cert_rotation: auto
  health: /healthz
```

Sam T.: That looks reasonable. One more thing: fallback behaviour when CP can't be reached. For some customers we need offline inference for a short window (cached KV + pinned models). Where does that logic live? edge-proxy or runtime?

Rachel B.: Runtime should be able to serve cached requests; edge-proxy can return `503` with a `Retry-After` if the runtime indicates degraded. control-agent should coordinate a controlled failover policy (can mark node read-only).

Maria N.: About networking patterns: do we prefer VPC peering or PrivateLink for control plane? Peering is simpler for high throughput but leaks routes. PrivateLink gives explicit endpoint and is auditable.

Alex K.: Decision criteria we used earlier still stand: PrivateLink for enterprise customers requiring minimal routing changes + auditability; peering for low-latency, high-throughput internal customers. But connector roles should be agnostic — both must support either.

Sam T.: Implementation note: for PrivateLink we need to ensure `edge-proxy` can reach customer endpoints by DNS name (no NAT), so we should ship a DNS resolver config option and a fallback to use customer-supplied route table via the control-agent.

Rachel B.: Also flagging TCO: more moving parts means higher support surface. We should minimize optional toggles: default to safe mode (control-agent manages creds) and advanced customers can opt into direct peering optimizations.

Alex K.: Plan for RFC follow-up:
- write short interface spec for `edge-proxy <-> control-agent` (socket API + proto)
- add cert rotation SLOs and a do-no-disrupt test in staging
- build a small migration playbook for peering -> privatelink and vice-versa

Maria N.: I'll draft the interface spec. Quick Q: preferred wire proto — unix domain + HTTP/JSON or gRPC?

Sam T.: gRPC for health/controls (bidirectional streams), keep a tiny HTTP JSON shim for human debugging.

Rachel B.: Ops will add a canary with `conn_pool.max=50` and observe cache stability. I'll own rollout steps. :thumbsup:

deploy-bot: deploy queued for `connector-prototype` -> staging (build 0.1.3). CI: 14/16 checks passed.

Alex K.: Thanks everyone. Maria, tag me on the spec PR and we can get this into RFC state.

Maria N.: Will do. Filing PR in ~30m.
